item.title: Cognitive Science Weekly: week of 2026-10-26
item.description:
Two papers this week bear on how language handles noise: a review arguing that noisy-channel inference explains both the robustness and the occasional breakdown of comprehension, and experiments on referring expressions in which listeners sometimes reinterpreted unambiguous zero anaphors as ambiguous pronouns when the event made that reading more plausible, especially under noise. The same experiments found speakers using more explicit forms for surprising events, which supports audience design. A second thread concerns what is domain-general versus domain-specific in learning and development. A proposal for replacing core knowledge accounts explains infant expectation-violation effects through attentional biases and perceptual prediction error, while work on toddlers' modal reasoning found much stronger performance when uncertainty concerned an object's kind rather than its location. Three experiments on auditory and visual categories found no sign of abstract representations shared across modalities, even with explicit instructions to draw analogies. Among the more surprising results, studies of task switching found smaller switch costs when people chose their own task, driven by faster switch-trial responses, and a scanpath analysis of Hebrew word reading found that longer words prompted more serial processing whether or not they were familiar. Finally, two preregistered experiments on judgments of learning found a memory cost for unrelated pairs without reliable changes in restudy decisions, which weakens the changed-goal explanation.

  • An Integrated Account of Language Comprehension and Processing as Noisy-Channel Inference
  • Successful modal reasoning depends on WHAT went WHERE
  • Selection-for-prediction: rethinking early cognitive development
  • Event predictability modulates production and comprehension of referring expressions
  • Enhanced cognitive flexibility with self-determined task choice.
  • Learners do not readily form abstract category representations across sensory modalities.
  • Are restudy decisions reactively altered by judgments of learning? Insights from related and unrelated word pairs
  • Serial or Parallel? Sublexical Scanpath Analysis of Eye-movement Sequences in Single Word Reading

item.title: Cognitive Science Weekly: week of 2026-10-19
item.description:
This week's papers keep asking whether an apparent specific deficit is really something more general. In a forced-response flanker study of over 200 younger and older adults, age differences in inhibitory control were explained by global slowing, with no selective inhibition deficit. Work on resampling rejected hypotheses found that attention control accounted for the working memory link, which suggests the problem is disengaging from outdated ideas rather than remembering a list of them. An interference framing also shows up in a study of language models on the N-back task, where the correct item could be located and decoded but the readout failed under interference. Suppressing competitor identity helped there, while sharpening attention didn't. On learning, a month-long study of four- to six-year-olds found that younger children seemed to relearn word regularities from scratch each time, while older children strengthened connections with each exposure. In contrast, a test of retrieval practice with novel words found better definition recall at 48 hours but no semantic priming, so no evidence that retrieval drives

  • Modeling working memory capacity in sentence processing with lossy-context surprisal
  • Dimensional asymmetries in social attention: Dynamic head movements elicit opposite attentional biases in vertical versus horizontal dimensions

item.title: Cognitive Science Weekly: week of 2026-10-12
item.description:
This week's papers share a concern with how robust a claimed mechanism or difference really is. A stress test of a connectome-constrained fly vision model found that circuit-level conclusions shift with the attribution method, the circuit representation, and the trained solution, and that some behavioral signatures also appear in matched CNNs. A similar caution runs through work on language models answering psychological scales, where a cross-language difference in trait was offset by a difference in response bias on scales without reverse-keyed items. A large sentence-picture experiment on scalar implicature likewise found that the predicted polarity effect varied across scales and was only weakly supported. On the more positive side, six preregistered studies of a Battleship-style game found that players randomized close to optimally in a competitive setting, which suggests that earlier claims about human randomization limits may depend on the tasks used. A framework that varies retrieval competition in Hopfield-like networks showed the same stored traces yielding different kinds of generalization, an argument for one flexible hippocampus-like system over separate memory systems. Among the developmental and clinical findings, pre-reading toddlers from English, Spanish and Hebrew communities showed naming directions that matched their culture's writing direction, and EEG entrainment to non-speech rhythms predicted dyslexia well, pointing to a phonemic entrainment deficit.

  • The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
  • Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
  • The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
  • Near-random behavior in strategic games
  • Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
  • Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
  • EEG Entrainment to Non-Speech Rhythmic Patterns Associated with Dimensions of Language Performance
  • FlyHack: Stress-Testing Mechanistic Claims in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model

item.title: Cognitive Science Weekly: week of 2026-10-11
item.description:
This week's papers cluster around how memory and attention are shaped by structure and by the limits of processing. Two memory studies show that later events can reshape what is retained: threat conditioning retroactively improved 24-hour recognition of the starting category in a sequence that ended in a shock-predictive category, and EEG evidence linked temporally guided attention shifts in working memory to long-term forgetting of the deprioritized item. A third memory study found that highly memorable images lose accuracy under short retrieval deadlines just as low-memorability images do, which favors a resource-dependent account over a resilience account. On the development side, children aged 9-10 showed independence between stability and flexibility rather than a trade-off, and successor knowledge, not approximate-magnitude mappings, predicted understanding of the later-greater principle. Two results stand out for the gap between model or normative predictions and human behavior: language models of varying architecture and size underestimated the human integration cost of long-distance subject-verb dependencies in a large self-paced reading dataset, and participants in the counterfactual decision study were far from optimal because of faulty inference, a weakness that statistical expertise did not remedy. A recurrent network account of perceptual grouping in natural scenes rounds out the set, with dynamics that predicted human reaction times.

  • Aversive learning retroactively modulates neutral episodic memories structured by prior knowledge of predictive sequences
  • Independent regulation of cognitive stability and flexibility in both intra-task and inter-task contexts among children
  • Temporal expectation triggers priority shifts in working memory that lead to forgetting
  • Memorability under pressure: Memorable images are not resilient to retrieval deadlines.
  • One, Two, Three, Four… What's More? Successor Relations, not Mappings to Approximate Magnitudes, Support Learning the Later‐Greater Principle
  • Recurrent network dynamics explain the time course of perceptual grouping in natural scenes
  • STRUCTURALCOST: A controlled reading time dataset for modeling human sentence processing difficulty
  • Making good decisions with counterfactuals
